After Athena won the contest and destroyed Arachne's web—which depicted the gods' misdeeds—Arachne attempted to hang herself [1]. Athena saved her from death but pronounced a cruel doom: Arachne would dangle on a cord forever, and her punishment would extend to all her descendants [1]. responses_by_run.answer: Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was an exceptionally skilled weaver who refused to acknowledge that her talent came from Athena's instruction [1]. When the goddess, disguised as an old woman, advised her to pray for Athena's pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected the advice and challenged the goddess to a weaving contest [1]. After Athena won the contest and destroyed Arachne's web—which depicted the gods' shameful deeds—she struck Arachne repeatedly [2]. In despair, Arachne attempted to hang herself, but Athena saved her life while pronouncing her doom: she would dangle on a cord forever as a spider, and her punishment would extend to all her descendants [2]. Athena then sprinkled her with magical herbs, causing her body to shrink and transform into a spider, condemning her to weave webs eternally [3].

Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions: stealing fire and giving it to humans [1], and for attempting to deceive Zeus during a dispute at Mecone by dividing sacrificial portions unfairly [2]. When Zeus discovered that Prometheus had hidden fire in a stalk of fennel and given it to mankind, he ordered Hephaestus to bind Prometheus to Mount Caucasus with inextricable bonds and set an eagle upon him to devour his liver daily, which would regenerate each night [1]. This severe punishment lasted many years until Heracles eventually released him [1].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus cried out for help from other Cyclopes, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and left him alone [1][2]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and had his men cling to the middle sheep while he himself clung to the belly of the largest ram [1][2]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, the men escaped hidden beneath the sheep and made their way to the ships [1][2].

At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the gods celebrated the marriage with feast and song on Mount Pelion [1]. Chiron gave Peleus an ashen spear as a wedding gift, and Poseidon gave him immortal horses named Balius and Xanthus [1]. The marriage resulted in the conception of Achilles, their son [1].

Demeter stopped the crops from growing because she was grieving over the abduction of her daughter [1]. She vowed that she would never let fruit spring out of the ground until she beheld her own fair-faced daughter with her eyes [1]. She remained so wrathful in her heart that no one of the gods could persuade her, and she stubbornly rejected all their words and gifts [2].
